paragraphs.text: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is an inherited nephropathy, usually of late onset, characterized mainly by fluid-filled cysts in the kidneys. It is genetically heterogeneous. Deltas (2001) noted that the disease caused by mutation in PKD1 and the disease caused by mutation in PKD2 cannot be told apart on clinical grounds. However, patients with PKD2 mutations have a milder course, with onset on average 10 to 20 years later and a lower probability of reaching end-stage renal failure. Mutations in PKD2 are thought to account for about 15% of ADPKD cases (Torra et al., 1999; Koptides et al., 1999).

paragraphs.text: Bachner et al. (1990) described a large 3-generation family with ADPKD and reduced expression. Ultrasonographic screening of 60 family members found 20 individuals, aged 10 to 80 years, with one or several cysts in only one kidney, and 7 individuals with cysts in both kidneys. Transmission of unilateral cysts appeared to be autosomal dominant, although there were some generation gaps. The authors concluded that the family had a form of ADPKD with reduced penetrance. They also considered other explanations, including 2 distinct hereditary diseases in the family, or a new mutation in one branch of the family together with a high frequency of isolated renal cysts.

paragraphs.text: Ravine et al. (1992) compared 18 families (285 affected members) with mutations at the PKD1 locus and 5 families (49 affected individuals) in which involvement of PKD1 could be excluded. Compared with PKD1 patients, the non-PKD1 patients: - lived longer (median survival 71.5 vs 56.0 years) - had a lower risk of progressing to renal failure (odds ratio 0.35) - were less likely to have hypertension (adjusted odds ratio 0.29) - were diagnosed at an older age (median 69.1 vs 44.8 years) - had fewer renal cysts at diagnosis Most PKD1 families had been ascertained through clinics treating patients with renal impairment, but no non-PKD1 family was identified through this source. The authors concluded that non-PKD1 ADPKD has a much milder phenotype and that its reported prevalence is probably an underestimate.

paragraphs.text: The European PKD1-PKD2 Study Group (Hateboer et al., 1999) compared clinical data from 333 people with PKD1 (31 families), 291 people with PKD2 (31 families), and 398 geographically matched controls. Median age at death or onset of ESRD was: - 53.0 years in PKD1 - 69.1 years in PKD2 - 78.0 years in controls Women with PKD2 had a significantly longer median survival than men (71.0 vs 67.3 years), whereas no sex effect was seen in PKD1. Median age at presentation with kidney failure was 74.0 years in PKD2 versus 54.3 years in PKD1. Compared with PKD1 patients, PKD2 patients were less likely to have hypertension (odds ratio 0.25), a history of urinary tract infection (odds ratio 0.50), or hematuria (odds ratio 0.59). The authors concluded that although PKD2 is milder than PKD1, it shortens overall life expectancy and cannot be regarded as benign.

The authors suggested that second-hit mutations could be a crucial event in cystogenesis in ADPKD type 2.
